section_title: Why does the Lord wash His disciples’ feet?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 1 It was now just before the Passover Feast, and Jesus knew that His hour had come to leave this world and return to the Father. Having loved His own who were in the world, He loved them to the very end. 2 The evening meal was underway, and the devil had already put into the heart of Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot, to betray Jesus. 3 Jesus knew that the Father had delivered all things into His hands, and that He had come from God and was returning to God. 4 So He got up from the supper, laid aside His outer garments, and wrapped a towel around His waist. 5 After that, He poured water into a basin and began to wash the disciples’ feet and dry them with the towel that was around Him.

6 He came to Simon Peter, who asked Him, “Lord, are You going to wash my feet?” 7 Jesus replied, “You do not realize now what I am doing, but later you will understand.” 8 “Never shall You wash my feet!” Peter told Him. Jesus answered, “Unless I wash you, you have no part with Me.” 9 “Then, Lord,” Simon Peter replied, “not only my feet, but my hands and my head as well!” 10 Jesus told him, “Whoever has already bathed needs only to wash his feet, and he will be completely clean. And you are clean, though not all of you.” 11 For He knew who would betray Him. That is why He said, “Not all of you are clean.”

12 When Jesus had washed their feet and put on His outer garments, He reclined with them again and asked, “Do you know what I have done for you? 13 You call Me Teacher and Lord, and rightly so, because I am. 14 So if I, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also should wash one another’s feet. 15 I have set you an example so that you should do as I have done for you. 16 Truly, truly, I tell you, no servant is greater than his master, nor is a messenger greater than the one who sent him. 17 If you know these things, you will be blessed if you do them.

context_lines: Jesus knows that His hour has come and that He will return to the Father. John introduces the meal by speaking of His enduring love for His own. Knowing that the Father has placed all things in His hands, Jesus takes a towel and basin and washes the disciples’ feet. His authority is expressed through service.

Peter objects to receiving this service from his Lord. When Jesus tells him that receiving His washing is necessary to having a part with Him, Peter asks for his hands and head to be washed too. Jesus answers with the difference between someone who has bathed and the washing of the feet.

The word for bathed is λούω, louō (LOO-oh). [Thayer’s lexicon](https://biblehub.com/greek/3068.htm) distinguishes bathing the whole body from the word used here for washing a part of it. This helps us follow the conversation, but the vocabulary alone does not settle every question about the cleansing Jesus gives. John makes clear that more than bodily dirt is involved: the exception to being clean concerns the betrayer.

Jesus then explains the example. They rightly call Him Teacher and Lord; His service shows how they are to treat one another. The servant is not greater than the master, and knowing what He has done is to lead to doing it. The scene joins receiving His care with learning to give humble care to others.
common_interpretation_lines: Christians commonly understand the act as both humble service and a sign of the cleansing received from Jesus. [Wesley on verses 8–10](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-gospel-according-to-st-john/) emphasizes receiving His cleansing and walking in holiness; [Calvin on verse 10](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/john/13.htm) emphasizes the continuing renewal of His followers. The [Catholic bishops’ note on verse 10](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/john/13) also notes a possible connection with baptism.

Traditions differ over how to practice the example. The Catholic Church’s [2016 decree on washing feet](https://www.vatican.va/roman_curia/congregations/ccdds/documents/rc_con_ccdds_doc_20160106_decreto-lavanda-piedi_en.html) describes a rite at the Mass of the Lord’s Supper on Holy Thursday that represents Christ’s humility and love. It does not replace the continuing call to serve.

Mennonite Church USA’s [Confession of Faith, Article 13](https://www.mennoniteusa.org/who-are-mennonites/what-we-believe/confession-of-faith/foot-washing/), encourages washing one another’s feet when it meaningfully expresses service and love. The document explicitly acknowledges that some congregations practice it and others do not.

Wesley’s note on verse 14 understands the command as every kind of lowly service, rather than a requirement to repeat the particular action. Calvin, in verses 14–15, likewise emphasizes continuing service and objects to treating a ceremony alone as fulfillment of the example. These are the named teachers’ explanations, not a claim that every Methodist or Reformed congregation follows one practice.
god_plan_lines: The towel and basin fit the larger shape of Christ’s mission. [Philippians 2:5–11](https://biblehub.com/bsb/philippians/2.htm) describes the One equal with God taking the form of a servant and humbling Himself even to death on a cross. His service here gives the disciples a concrete example of that self-giving love.

The cleansing also points beyond washing skin. [Hebrews 9:11–14](https://biblehub.com/bsb/hebrews/9.htm) describes Christ’s offering of Himself as cleansing the conscience so that people may serve the living God. Jesus brings people into a relationship in which they receive His cleansing and learn His way of service.
